candidates.statement: This guidance specifically outlines clinical pharmacology considerations for development 22 programs for proposed peptide drug products submitted in a new drug application (NDA) under 23 section 505(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) and references other 24 relevant guidances when appropriate. The term peptide , for purposes of this guidance, refers to 25 any polymer composed of 40 or fewer amino acids. 2 In general, if a peptide meets the definition 26 of a drug and does not otherwise meet the statutory definition of a “biological product” 3 or a 27 “device,” 4 it would be regulated as a drug under the FD&C Act and be subject to all the “drug” 28 requirements under the FD&C Act and FDA’s regulations, including the requirement that new 29 drugs must be approved under section 505(c) of the FD&C Act before they can be marketed in 30 interstate commerce. 5 However, peptide drug products can have product characteristics that may 31 be similar, in certain respects, to biological products, and as such, this guidance includes 32 references to other FDA guidances on biological products that discuss scientific principles that 33 could also be applicable to peptide drug products. 34
candidates.context: This guidance provides recommendations to assist industry in the development of peptide drug 16 products. Specifically, this guidance, when finalized, will describe the FDA’s current thinking 17 regarding the impact of clinical pharmacology considerations, including hepatic impairment, 18 drug-drug interactions (DDIs), QTc prolongation risk, and immunogenicity risk on a peptide 19 drug product’s pharmacokinetics (PK), safety, and efficacy. 20 1 This guidance has been prepared by the Office of Clinical Pharmacology in the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research at the Food and Drug Administration.

candidates.statement: Peptides can be isolated from animal tissue, produced synthetically, or produced through 36 recombinant expression, and often serve as signaling molecules for many physiological 37 functions. Recent drug development efforts have focused on improving the absorption, 38 distribution, metabolism, and excretion (ADME) properties of native peptides, such as increasing 39 oral bioavailability, increasing half-life, decreasing general hydrophobicity, and increasing 40 conformational flexibility to increase selectivity of the intended target. To obtain more favorable 41 ADME characteristics in patients, peptide drug products under development have included 42 certain alterations to the peptide structure and/or incorporated new formulation strategies (e.g., 43 liposomes). These structural alterations can include cyclization, pseudo-peptide bonds, unnatural 44 amino acids, and peptide conjugations (e.g., PEGylation). As such, peptide drug products can 45 exhibit distinct combinations of characteristics of both small and large molecules regarding their 46 chemistry, pharmacology, pharmacokinetic disposition, and pharmacodynamics (PD). Of note, 47 this guidance does not focus on the development of any particular peptide drug product. Any 48 questions about regulatory requirements for a particular peptide drug product should be 49 addressed to the appropriate FDA review division. 50

candidates.statement: Most peptide drug products have the potential for immunogenicity; as such, sponsors should 86 generally assess the immunogenicity risk for all peptide drug products. Assessing the 87 immunogenicity risk for peptide drug products is similar to therapeutic proteins and involves 88 understanding certain product-specific factors (e.g., molecular size and structure), process- 89 specific factors (e.g., host cell proteins), subject-specific factors (e.g., disease state), and factors 90 related to study design and product use (e.g., dosing regimen, route(s) of administration, and 91 concomitant drugs). Factors related to immunogenicity risk of peptides are consistent with the 92 scientific principles outlined in the FDA guidance for industry entitled Immunogenicity 93 Assessment for Therapeutic Protein Products (August 2014) . In general, peptide drug products 94 that are less than eight amino acids are not expected to be immunogenic unless there is an 95 immunogenicity risk due to product impurities or aggregates. 96

candidates.statement: The clinical immunogenicity assessment should be designed to assess the clinical impact of 120 ADAs on the peptide drug product’s PK, PD, efficacy, and safety. Specifically, both between- 121 subject (i.e., between subjects who test ADA positive and those who test ADA negative) and 122 within-subject comparisons (i.e., before ADA positive and after ADA positive) should be 123 assessed. For all individual subjects who test ADA positive, further evaluation on the effects of 124 antibody titers and neutralizing antibodies on the peptide drug product’s PK, PD, efficacy, and 125 safety should be assessed. 126

candidates.statement: • Peptide drug products that are being developed for an indication with the liver as a target 161 organ or in cases when the peptide drug product can be characterized as targeting the 162 liver (e.g., GalNAc residues in the molecule) could be affected by hepatic impairment. As 163 changes in liver function can result in pharmacodynamic changes that are independent of 164 systemic pharmacokinetic changes, whenever appropriate and feasible, 165 pharmacodynamic assessments should be included. 166

candidates.context: In general, peptide drug products are primarily metabolized by proteolytic or hydrolytic enzymes 190 such as endopeptidases, aminopeptidases, and carboxypeptidases, or are chemically modified to 191 resist degradation, and are not metabolized by cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes. Therefore, the 192 disposition of peptide drug products is not anticipated to be affected by inhibitors or inducers of 193 CYP enzymes. Similarly, modulation of efflux transporters, such as P-gp and BCRP, or hepatic 194 uptake transporters such as OATP1B1 and OATP1B3, or renal uptake or efflux transporters, 195 such as OAT1, OAT3, OCT2, MATE1, and MATE2/K are generally not anticipated to have a 196 significant impact on the PK of peptide drug products. candidates.statement: However, there are structural modifications to peptide drug products, such as cyclic peptides 201 (e.g., cyclosporine and voclosporin) that could render them susceptible to CYP enzyme-mediated 202 metabolism and transporter-mediated disposition. In vitro experiments related to CYPs and 203 transporters may be scientifically appropriate when hepatic and/or biliary excretion accounts for 204 >20 percent of the overall elimination and/or the drug’s target organ is the liver. For more 205 information, see the FDA guidance entitled In Vitro Drug Interaction Studies — Cytochrome 206 P450 Enzyme- and Transporter-Mediated Drug Interactions Guidance for Industry (January 207 2020). Additionally, in vitro experiments to evaluate a drug as a substrate of renal transporters 208 may be appropriate for drugs with renal active secretion that accounts for >25 percent of 209 systemic clearance of the drug and/or a drug that has renal toxicity. Sponsors should provide 210 their plans and rationale early in development to evaluate whether peptide drug products are 211 substrates of CYP enzymes and drug transporters. 212
candidates.context: When final, this guidance will represent the Agency’s current thinking on this topic. b. Peptide drug products as inhibitors and inducers of CYP enzymes and 214 transporters 215

candidates.statement: In general, peptide drug products are not expected to significantly modulate CYP enzymes and 217 drug transporters. However, there are structural modifications to peptide drug products (e.g., 218 cyclosporine and voclosporin) that could lead to modulation of CYP enzymes and drug 219 transporters. In addition, there are cases where peptides indirectly affect CYP enzymes or 220 transporters. One example is somatostatin analogs (e.g., lanreotide and octreotide) that reduce or 221 are suspected to reduce the clearance of co-administered drugs indirectly by modulating the 222 expression of CYP enzymes. For each development program, sponsors should provide their plans 223 to evaluate the drug interaction liability of peptide drug products, as recommended in the FDA 224 guidance entitled In Vitro Drug Interaction Studies — Cytochrome P450 Enzyme- and 225 Transporter-Mediated Drug Interactions Guidance for Industry (January 2020). Regarding the 226 recommendations for clinical assessment of DDIs, refer to the FDA guidance entitled Clinical 227 Drug Interaction Studies — Cytochrome P450 Enzyme- and Transporter-Mediated Drug 228 Interactions Guidance for Industry (January 2020). 229
candidates.context: b. Peptide drug products as inhibitors and inducers of CYP enzymes and 214 transporters 215 Additionally, certain peptide drug products could alter the PK of concomitant drugs as a result of 231 their mechanism of action. For example, glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists (e.g., 232 exenatide and liraglutide) could delay gastric emptying of co-administered oral drugs. Also, in 233 situations where the mechanism of action of the peptide drug product could affect the PK of co- 234 administered products, the sponsor should evaluate the peptide drug product as a perpetrator. 235

candidates.statement: When indicated, an assessment of QTc prolongation risk and a proposed QTc assessment plan 252 should be submitted as described in the FDA guidances entitled E14 Clinical Evaluation of 253 QT/QTc Interval Prolongation and Proarrhythmic Potential for Non-Antiarrhythmic Drugs 254 (October 2012), the E14 Clinical Evaluation of QT/QTc Interval Prolongation and 255 Proarrhythmic Potential for Non-Antiarrhythmic Drugs Questions and Answers (R3) (June 256 2017), and E14 and S7B Clinical and Nonclinical Evaluation of QT/QTc Interval Prolongation 257 and Proarrhythmic Potential--Questions and Answers ( August 2022 ). All proposals in the QTc 258 assessment plan should contain a rationale and be discussed with the Agency. The timing and 259 extent of the clinical QTc assessment depend upon the overall risk/benefit profile of the peptide 260 drug product. 261

candidates.statement: Given the potential for immunogenicity generally associated with peptide drug product 286 administration, the labeling for such products should include immunogenicity information, 287 consistent with the principles proposed in FDA’s draft guidance Immunogenicity Information in 288 Human Prescription Therapeutic Protein and Select Drug Product Labeling — Content and 289 Format (February 2022). 16 In general, the labeling for peptide drug products that are less than 290 eight amino acids that are without concerns for impurities and/or aggregates do not need to 291 include immunogenicity information because an immunogenicity assessment would likely not be 292 relevant to the assessment of a drug’s safety and effectiveness. 17
